Precedent

/PRESS-uh-duhnt/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Precedent means an earlier event, decision, or action that serves as an example or guide for later, similar situations — especially in law.

Precedent means an earlier event or decision that serves as an example or guide for later, similar situations — especially in law. Before issuing her ruling, the judge searched for a precedent from earlier cases like this one.

Worked Example

By letting one student retake the exam, the professor set a precedent that the rest of the class soon invoked.

The professor's first decision became a guide: later students pointed back to it and expected the same treatment. An earlier decision used as a model for later ones is a precedent.

How Precedent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

example

example: a case that shows how something can be done

model

model: a pattern that later actions are based on

benchmark

benchmark: a reference point that later things are measured against

Antonyms

anomaly

anomaly: a one-time oddity that sets no pattern for the future

novelty

novelty: something entirely new, with no earlier example behind it

How Strong Is It? — example → landmark → precedent

example vs. precedent

example vs. precedent: Example is weaker — anything can serve as an example once; a precedent is an earlier decision that later decision-makers feel guided, even bound, to follow.

landmark vs. precedent

landmark vs. precedent: Landmark is stronger — a landmark case doesn't just guide later decisions, it reshapes the entire field of law around it.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of precedent.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before, in advance (Latin prae-)

Root — ced

Root — ced: to go, to move (Latin cedere)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: that which does (noun/adjective ending)

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- ('before') + cedere ('to go') builds 'that which goes before.' A precedent is the case that went first — and later decisions walk the path it opened.

Use the root in a new word: concede

Use the root in a new word: concede: Trailing by twenty points with a minute left, the coach finally had to concede the match — literally to 'go along' with the other side.

Word Choice

Formal / legal

Precedent lives in fixed phrases: 'set a precedent,' 'follow precedent,' 'without precedent' (and the adjective 'unprecedented'). Careful: this unit also teaches precedence — a different word meaning priority or higher rank ('safety takes precedence over speed'). A precedent is a past example; precedence is who or what comes first in importance. Never swap them.
